propositions.text: Once Crown establishes conditions, burden shifts to accused to raise reasonable doubt about breathalyzer reliability.
If no evidence raises doubt, breathalyzer results presumed accurate and reflect blood alcohol level at testing and material time.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that once the Crown establishes conditions, the accused must raise reasonable doubt about breathalyzer reliability; otherwise, results are presumed accurate.

propositions.text: Appeal concerns scope of evidence needed to rebut presumptions of accuracy and identity under s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C.
Court allowed Crown's appeal, set aside acquittal, ordered new trial, and provides reasons here.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the appeal concerns evidence scope to rebut breathalyzer presumptions and that it allowed Crown's appeal, ordering a new trial with reasons.

propositions.text: Burden on accused to rebut presumptions has been debated but settled by R. v. St-Onge Lamoureux.
Accused must show malfunction or improper operation casts doubt on breathalyzer reliability (St-Onge Lamoureux).
New provisions recognize reliability depends on proper operation and maintenance; deficiencies must relate directly to reliability.
Requirement ensures scientific recognition and proper functioning of breathalyzer instruments (St-Onge Lamoureux).

paragraphs.summary: The court states that R. v. St-Onge Lamoureux settled that accused must show malfunction or improper operation casts doubt on breathalyzer reliability.

propositions.text: Accused discharges burden if adduces evidence of malfunction and shows defect tends to cast doubt on reliability.
Each condition has theoretical and practical elements: procedure generally required and not followed; defect affects reliability.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains accused must show malfunction and that defect tends to cast doubt, each with theoretical and practical elements.

propositions.text: No need to decide if improper operation established here; no evidence defect cast doubt on reliability.
Court of Appeal's judgment reversed; Superior Court's order for new trial restored.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence defect cast doubt on reliability and reverses Court of Appeal, restoring Superior Court's new trial order.

propositions.text: Respondent stopped July 12, 2012, arrested, taken to station, observed by officers during call to counsel.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes respondent's arrest and observation by officers during call to counsel on July 12, 2012.

propositions.text: First breathalyzer test at 1:08 a.m. showed 157 mg alcohol; second at 1:30 a.m. showed 148 mg; both over legal limit.
Respondent charged with impaired driving and blood alcohol over 80 mg; only second charge at issue.

paragraphs.summary: The court states respondent's two breathalyzer tests showed over legal limit and only second charge is at issue.

propositions.text: At trial, parties agreed to determine if technician breached duty by failing to observe accused for 15 or 20 minutes before tests.
Accused argued breach rebutted presumptions, requiring acquittal absent Crown evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes parties agreed trial would address technician's observation duty breach and accused argued breach rebutted presumptions.

propositions.text: Only technician testified; trial judge found technician not required to observe accused himself; observation by another officer was not continuous.
Trial judge found failure to follow observation procedure raised reasonable doubt on reliability without additional evidence.
Respondent acquitted of second charge; Crown had no evidence on first charge.

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found observation procedure not followed continuously, raising reasonable doubt, and acquitted respondent of second charge.

propositions.text: Crown appealed, arguing evidence insufficient to rebut presumptions.
Superior Court allowed appeal, set aside acquittal, ordered new trial, citing R. v. So principles.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown appealed; Superior Court allowed appeal, set aside acquittal, and ordered new trial citing R. v. So.

propositions.text: R. v. So summarized accused's burden: prove deficiency in instrument and that deficiency relates to reliability to reasonable doubt standard.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites R. v. So summarizing accused's burden to prove deficiency and its relation to reliability to reasonable doubt.

propositions.text: Respondent sought leave to appeal to Court of Appeal on question of law; leave granted.
Majority of Court of Appeal set aside Superior Court judgment, restored acquittal verdict.
All judges agreed accused must show improper operation and evidence tending to show it could influence result.
Majority found determination was factual and Superior Court erred absent unreasonable evidence assessment.
Dissent would have upheld Superior Court, finding no evidence deficiency could affect result.

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal majority restored acquittal, finding accused must show improper operation and influence on result; dissent upheld Superior Court.

propositions.text: Issue is how accused can show defect tends to cast doubt on reliability when instrument operated improperly.
Dispute is whether purely theoretical evidence suffices to raise doubt on reliability.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the issue as whether theoretical evidence suffices to show defect casts doubt on breathalyzer reliability.

propositions.text: Abstract evidence alone unlikely to meet reasonable doubt requirement; concrete evidence usually required.
Without concrete evidence, accused's argument is speculation and fails reasonable doubt test (St-Onge Lamoureux).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds abstract evidence insufficient and concrete evidence usually required to meet reasonable doubt standard.

propositions.text: Respondent's argument that theoretical defect suffices is rejected as mere hypothetical possibility, insufficient for reasonable doubt.
Respondent was searched twice, monitored, and test results consistent, so digestive issues affecting results unlikely.
Improper operation alleged did not tend to show reliability doubt; minimum evidence not adduced.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects respondent's theoretical argument, noting consistent tests and monitoring, finding no evidence of reliability doubt.

propositions.text: Improper operation may sometimes alone raise reasonable doubt if serious or closely connected to reliability.
Dissenting judge noted concrete evidence needed to link improper operation to results, not mere hypothesis.
Court of Québec judge pointed to no concrete evidence beyond speculation; Superior Court correctly found no evidence casting doubt.
Court of Appeal majority erred in reversing Superior Court decision.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with dissent that concrete evidence is needed; finds no evidence here and that Court of Appeal majority erred.

propositions.text: Intervener argues accused cannot testify about alcohol consumption or digestive problems without contravening s. 258(1)(d.01) Cr. C.
Court rejects intervener's argument; accused can testify about digestive problems as concrete evidence affecting reliability after identifying defect.
Challenges to presumptions under s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C. relate only to instrument functioning and operation.
Testimonial evidence admissible but not compulsory.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects intervener's argument, allowing accused to testify about digestive problems as concrete evidence affecting reliability.

propositions.text: Respondent denies presenting a 'burping defence' as it relates to s. 258(1)(d.1) Cr. C.
Court finds burping defence was central to respondent's argument that improper operation cast doubt on reliability due to unnoticed digestive issues.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds respondent's burping defence was central to his argument that improper operation cast doubt on reliability.

propositions.text: No evidence showed defect cast doubt on reliability; defect cannot form basis for reasonable doubt.
Acceptance of theoretical evidence reflects misinterpretation of accused's burden, an error of law.
Superior Court did not err in setting aside acquittal and ordering new trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no evidence of reliability doubt, rejects theoretical evidence, and upholds Superior Court's new trial order.

propositions.text: R. v. St-Onge Lamoureux held evidentiary scheme infringes s. 11(d) Charter right to presumption of innocence.
Infringement justified partly due to recognized reliability of breathalyzer results contingent on proper functioning and operation.
If accused raises reasonable doubt about functioning or operation, presumptions under s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C. must be discarded.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites St-Onge Lamoureux that evidentiary scheme infringes presumption of innocence but justified by breathalyzer reliability contingent on proper operation.

propositions.text: Trial judge found technician's testimony showed observation period before breathalyzer was not complied with, raising reasonable doubt about reliability
Trial judge made no error of law warranting appellate intervention
Issue is weighing evidence; acquittal must be upheld

paragraphs.summary: The trial judge found technician's testimony raised reasonable doubt about breathalyzer reliability; court finds no legal error and upholds acquittal.

propositions.text: Majority requires evidence that improper breathalyzer operation led to inaccurate results, e.g., accused's physiological reactions
Such requirement would upset balance between accused's constitutional rights and Parliament's objectives
Coupled with Gubbins decision excluding breathalyzer maintenance records from first party disclosure, this requirement would make defences illusory

paragraphs.summary: Court argues majority's requirement for concrete evidence of inaccuracy would upset rights-objectives balance and make defences illusory, citing Gubbins.

propositions.text: Will discuss St-Onge Lamoureux reasoning, clarify defence and Crown burdens, consider case facts, and conclude on fairness of new trial

paragraphs.summary: Court outlines plan to discuss St-Onge Lamoureux, clarify burdens, analyze facts, and conclude on new trial fairness.

propositions.text: Appeal requires considering accused's burden to counter presumptions in s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C. and evidence needed

paragraphs.summary: Appeal concerns burden on accused to counter statutory presumptions and required evidence.

propositions.text: Position based on majority reasons in St-Onge Lamoureux and Gubbins
Majority acknowledges St-Onge Lamoureux but departs from it
Validity of evidentiary scheme upheld partly because accused could raise reasonable doubt about breathalyzer operation

paragraphs.summary: Court bases position on St-Onge Lamoureux and Gubbins, notes majority departs from St-Onge Lamoureux which allowed reasonable doubt on breathalyzer operation.

propositions.text: Scientific evidence in St-Onge Lamoureux showed breathalyzer reliability but importance of following procedures for accuracy
Expert evidence shows real possibility of instrument malfunction or improper use
Human error can occur in sample taking and maintenance
Hodgson's report emphasizes proper operation and maintenance for scientifically sound results

paragraphs.summary: St-Onge Lamoureux scientific evidence showed breathalyzer reliability but real risk of malfunction and human error, emphasizing proper operation and maintenance.

propositions.text: Court gave example of observation period before test as relevant procedure for reliability
Alcohol Test Committee recommends 15-minute observation before breath sample
Reference to R. v. Drolet for similar procedural requirements

paragraphs.summary: Court cited Alcohol Test Committee's 15-minute observation recommendation and Drolet case as relevant procedures for breathalyzer reliability.

propositions.text: Constitutionality depends on possibility and ease for accused to rebut presumption

paragraphs.summary: Court emphasized constitutionality depends on accused's ability to rebut presumption.

propositions.text: Only first requirement in s. 258(1)(c) to show malfunction or improper operation is reasonable limit on presumption of innocence
Burden justified because results reliable only if instruments properly operated and maintained

paragraphs.summary: Court found only first requirement to show malfunction or improper operation is reasonable and justified burden on accused.

propositions.text: Court declined to define nature and scope of evidence to show improper operation
Deschamps J. noted relevance of Alcohol Test Committee recommendations for ensuring proper function

paragraphs.summary: Court did not define evidence needed to show improper operation but noted Alcohol Test Committee recommendations' relevance.

propositions.text: Possibility to show procedures not followed means reliability cannot be assumed
First requirement in s. 258(1)(c) justified under s. 1 Charter
This conclusion clarifies accused's burden to counter presumptions

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes accused can show procedures not followed to rebut reliability; first requirement justified and clarifies accused's burden.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux did not elevate recommendations to statutory conditions Crown must meet
Only statutory conditions in s. 258(1)(c)(ii) to (iv) apply

paragraphs.summary: Court states only statutory conditions in s. 258(1)(c)(ii)-(iv) apply; recommendations are not statutory conditions.

propositions.text: Quebec Court of Appeal majority held accused bears burden to show malfunction or improper operation that could affect reliability
Accused not required to show results are actually inaccurate
Evidence need only raise reasonable doubt (St-Onge Lamoureux, Gibson)

paragraphs.summary: Quebec Court of Appeal held accused must show malfunction or improper operation raising reasonable doubt about reliability, not actual inaccuracy.

propositions.text: Burden formulation consistent with St-Onge Lamoureux requiring evidence of defect casting doubt on reliability
Consistent with R. v. So principles

paragraphs.summary: Burden to show defect casting doubt on reliability aligns with St-Onge Lamoureux and R. v. So.

propositions.text: Majority claims burden is to raise reasonable doubt about reliability by evidence of malfunction or improper operation
Majority requires evidence concretely related to facts, effectively requiring accused to cast doubt on accuracy
This is contrary to St-Onge Lamoureux which rejected second requirement linking deficiency to results

paragraphs.summary: Court criticizes majority for effectively requiring accused to prove inaccuracy, contrary to St-Onge Lamoureux's rejection of such burden.

propositions.text: St-Onge Lamoureux requires reasonable doubt about reliability, not accuracy
Reliability means system's ability to function without incident; accuracy means conformity to truth
Distinction between reliability and accuracy is significant

paragraphs.summary: Court explains distinction between reliability and accuracy is significant; St-Onge Lamoureux requires doubt about reliability, not accuracy.

propositions.text: Evidence showing malfunction or improper operation increasing possibility of inaccuracy meets accused's burden
Accused need not show direct reasonable doubt about accuracy on case facts
Sufficient to show recommended procedure not followed and its purpose is to ensure reliability
This is a defect casting doubt on reliability under St-Onge Lamoureux
Accused's burden ends there; presumptions justified only if procedures complied with

paragraphs.summary: Accused meets burden by showing procedure not followed affecting reliability; no need to prove inaccuracy; burden ends there.

propositions.text: Burden shifts to Crown to prove beyond reasonable doubt deficiency did not impact accuracy
Reverse onus not excessive per St-Onge Lamoureux
If Crown fails, loses benefit of presumptions
Crown should not rely on technician rigour to prove reliability then trivialize it when challenged

paragraphs.summary: Burden shifts to Crown to prove no impact on accuracy; failure loses presumptions; applicant argues Crown should not trivialize technician rigour.

propositions.text: Accused may rely solely on qualified technician's testimony to raise reasonable doubt about reliability
Evidence to counter presumptions may come from Crown or defence witnesses

paragraphs.summary: Accused can rely solely on qualified technician's testimony to raise reasonable doubt; evidence may come from Crown or defence witnesses.

propositions.text: Qualified technician responsible for proper breathalyzer operation under Criminal Code
Technician's testimony about procedure purpose and failure to follow it can raise reasonable doubt alone
Accused not required to provide additional evidence to corroborate technician's testimony
Opposite position disregards Parliament's unique role for qualified technicians in blood alcohol analysis

paragraphs.summary: Technician's testimony alone can raise reasonable doubt; accused need not corroborate; disregarding this ignores Parliament's role for technicians.

propositions.text: Trier of fact must assess evidence to determine if it counters statutory presumptions.
Qualified technician’s testimony alone may not raise reasonable doubt if problems are trivial.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the trier of fact must assess evidence to counter presumptions; technician's testimony may be insufficient if problems are trivial.

propositions.text: Trial judge correctly stated law requiring accused to show breathalyzer malfunction or improper operation raising reasonable doubt about test reliability.
Trial judge's factual findings are supported by evidence.
Verdict of acquittal is unimpeachable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge correctly stated law, supported by evidence, and the acquittal verdict is unimpeachable.

propositions.text: Crown argues deprivation of presumptions was due to mere speculative possibility.
Crown failed to identify legal error warranting intervention.
Deprivation of presumptions was due to concrete evidence of procedural deficiency affecting reliability.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Crown's argument of speculative possibility is incorrect; deprivation of presumptions was due to concrete evidence, no legal error found.

propositions.text: Disagrees with majority that trial judge misinterpreted reasonable doubt or based findings on speculation.
Reasonable doubt must relate to improper breathalyzer operation affecting reliability, not blood alcohol level or accuracy.
Evidence in this case was not theoretical.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with majority on reasonable doubt interpretation, clarifies its scope, and finds evidence was not theoretical.

propositions.text: Majority concedes improper operation evidence may raise reasonable doubt about reliability.
Sufficiency of evidence to raise reasonable doubt is for trier of fact to decide.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes majority concedes improper operation evidence may raise reasonable doubt; trier of fact decides sufficiency of evidence.

propositions.text: Mr. Cyr-Langlois adduced relevant evidence of improper breathalyzer operation.
Trial judge found evidence sufficient to raise reasonable doubt about reliability.
Court should not intervene.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Cyr-Langlois adduced sufficient evidence raising reasonable doubt and decides not to intervene.

propositions.text: Constable Boissonneault stated prescribed procedure includes 20-minute observation to prevent residual mouth alcohol.
Testimony sufficiently shows procedure exists to ensure test reliability.
No need to file training manual or expert testimony to corroborate witness.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the technician's testimony about a 20-minute observation procedure sufficiently shows its existence without needing manuals or experts.

propositions.text: Boissonneault did not observe accused himself; another officer did but could not confirm continuous observation.
Accused was alone in soundproof room during part of observation period exercising right to counsel.
Boissonneault acknowledged responsibility but was unconcerned about observation gaps.
Trial judge could find technician’s testimony sufficient to raise reasonable doubt about observation compliance.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds gaps in observation and technician's unconcern support trial judge's finding of reasonable doubt about compliance.

propositions.text: Trial judge could find evidence showed improper breathalyzer operation affecting reliability, not mere possibility.
Qualified technician administered tests without following prescribed procedure or ensuring no physiological reactions.
Trial judge could reasonably doubt test reliability.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds trial judge reasonably doubted reliability due to improper operation, not mere possibility or speculation.

propositions.text: Accused discharged burden under s. 258(1)(c) Cr. C. by raising reasonable doubt about breathalyzer operation.
Hogue J.A. held trial judge did not need further evidence from accused to deny presumptions to prosecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds accused met burden to raise reasonable doubt; Hogue J.A. supports no further evidence needed from accused.

propositions.text: Requiring accused to testify about alcohol consumption and physiological reactions would infringe rights.
Majority’s approach improperly shifts burden to accused to observe and testify about physiological reactions.
State, not accused, must ensure conditions for accurate breathalyzer results.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds requiring accused testimony infringes rights and that state must ensure accurate breathalyzer conditions, not accused.

propositions.text: Majority suggests test result consistency shows observation failure had no impact, confirming reliability.
Onus was on Crown to prove no impact, which it failed to do.
Presumptions of accuracy and identity were discarded; trial judge had to acquit.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Crown failed to prove no impact of observation failure; presumptions discarded and acquittal required.

propositions.text: Even if Crown’s new arguments were accepted, court would hesitate to order new trial.
Intervener notes Crown’s appellate position differs from trial position.

paragraphs.summary: The court would hesitate to order new trial given Crown’s changed position on appeal noted by intervener.

propositions.text: Crown prosecutor did not argue at trial that technician’s testimony alone was insufficient to counter presumptions.
Crown did not argue necessity of filing training manuals or accused’s testimony about consumption and reactions.
Prosecutor’s trial position was that accused was sufficiently observed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Crown did not argue at trial that technician’s testimony was insufficient or that manuals or accused testimony were needed.

propositions.text: Ordering new trial would give Crown second chance based on new appellate arguments.
Such result would violate double jeopardy principle.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds ordering new trial on new arguments would violate double jeopardy principle.

propositions.text: Trial judge made no reviewable error in finding reasonable doubt about breathalyzer operation and countering presumptions.
Agrees with Hogue J.A. that trial judge did not require further evidence from accused.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes trial judge made no error and agrees with Hogue J.A. that no further evidence was required from accused.

propositions.text: Majority’s approach unduly limits defences based on improper breathalyzer operation.
Such defences justify evidentiary scheme under s. 1 of the Charter for blood alcohol offences.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds majority unduly limits defences that justify evidentiary scheme under Charter s. 1 for blood alcohol offences.

propositions.text: Majority’s reasons rely on Crown arguments made first on appeal.
Ordering new trial would be inappropriate given circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds majority relies on new Crown arguments and that ordering new trial would be inappropriate.

propositions.text: Appeal dismissed; Côté J. dissenting.
Solicitors for parties and interveners listed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses appeal with dissent; solicitors for parties and interveners are listed.
